lesson.title: The -al Invariable Passport
lesson.subtitle: natural, central, formal, personal, internacional — adjectives that never change for gender in the singular

hook.title: Identical Spelling, Invariable Gender
hook.content: Look at natural, central, formal, personal, cultural: their singular spelling in Spanish is 100% identical to English! Even better, when -tion- sits inside an -al word ('international', 'traditional'), it simply becomes -cion-: internacional, tradicional!

pattern.title: One Form for Both el and la
pattern.content: Because -al adjectives end in the consonant -l rather than -o, they do not change for gender: el tren internacional and la organización internacional use the exact same adjective form.

exercises.meaning: natural, central, formal, personal, international, cultural
exercises.explanation: All six end in -al and stay unchanged for masculine vs feminine singular.

summary.outcome: Deploy -al cognates after masculine and feminine nouns without changing their singular ending.

use_example.german: Es un tren internacional y una tradición cultural.
use_example.english: It is an international train and a cultural tradition.

summary.takeaway: Spanish -al adjectives match English spelling and fit both masculine and feminine nouns.

natural.etymology_derivation: Latin nātūrālis. Words in -al have identical singular spelling in English and Spanish.

tren.context_phrase: Tomo el tren a las ocho.
tren.context_translation: I take the train at eight.

opinión.etymology_derivation: Latin opīniō. Like -ción, words in -sión and -ión are consistently feminine.

al.name: The -AL Invariable Passport
al.phonetic_rule: English adjectives ending in -al match Spanish -al /-ˈal/ with identical spelling and gender-invariable singular form.
al.historical_linguistics: Latin adjectival suffix -ālis ('pertaining to'). Both languages kept the spelling; Spanish stresses the final syllable.
al.philological_note: El plan natural, la idea natural: no gender change in the singular.
